terminal.description: A shell in your workspace. Run the two windows here; the old count comes up short, and by a different number each run.

tasks.title: Count the tickets of both windows
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 1`, write a class `Sold` that keeps a count of tickets, 0 at first, safe for both windows at once. `void add(int tickets)` adds `tickets` to the count, and `int count()` gives back the count. Both methods are `synchronized`.

Check holds the lock of a `Sold` itself while another thread calls `add`, and sees whether that thread waits for the lock; while it waits, Check adds 100 itself, then lets go and reads the count. It does the same for `count`, and it also has four threads add at once, many times over. A lost update shows on every run of Check, though your terminal may show one only now and then.
nextSteps: Read the parts of the lesson about the lost update and about synchronized.
Write Sold as the OldCount above it, with a private count.
Take the // off the Sold lines in main and run it a few times: the count is right every time.
hints: OldCount, above the tasks, shows what goes wrong: compare it with the lesson's part on why count++ is three steps.

Every object has a lock, and a method can ask for its object's lock before it runs: then two threads can never be inside it at once. A method that only reads needs the lock too, to see the latest value.
`private int count;`, `synchronized void add(int tickets) { count += tickets; }` and `synchronized int count() { return count; }`.

tasks.title: Number every ticket once
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 2`, write a class `Numbers` that hands out ticket numbers from an `AtomicInteger`, safe for any number of threads at once. Its constructor takes the `AtomicInteger`, which holds the last number given out. `int next()` adds 1 to it and gives back the new number, so no two calls ever get the same number.

Check hands `Numbers` an `AtomicInteger` of its own and reads the numbers `next` gives back, and the `AtomicInteger` afterwards. Then it runs many rounds in which four threads take numbers at the same moment, and counts the rounds where a number came out twice or went missing. A wrong `next` may give no clash in your terminal, by luck; Check runs enough rounds that it shows.
nextSteps: Read the part of the lesson about AtomicInteger.
Keep the AtomicInteger the constructor is given in a private final field.
Write next with one call on it.
Take the // off the Numbers lines in main and run it.
hints: The lesson's part on AtomicInteger has a table of its methods: some do one step, some do two in one.
A get followed by a set is two steps, and another thread can come between them: the lost update again. The method you want adds and gives back the new value in one step no thread can come between.
`private final AtomicInteger last;`, `this.last = last;` in the constructor, and `return last.incrementAndGet();` in next.

tasks.title: Add up the takings, printing outside the lock
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 3`, write a class `Takings` that keeps the takings, `BigDecimal.ZERO` at first. `void sell(BigDecimal fare, Printer printer)` prints the ticket with `printer.print(fare)`, then adds `fare` to the takings. Only the adding is guarded, by a `synchronized` block on the `Takings` itself: the printing is outside it, so a slow printer at one window never holds up the other. `BigDecimal total()` gives back the takings, and is `synchronized`. `Printer` is given above the tasks.

Check hands `sell` a printer of its own, which notes whether the thread printing holds the lock of the `Takings` at that moment. It holds that lock itself while another thread calls `sell` and sees whether the adding waits for it; while it waits, Check sells a ticket of its own, then lets go and compares the takings by their value. It also has four threads sell at once, many times over.
nextSteps: Read the part of the lesson about keeping the locked part small.
Write total as Task 1 wrote count.
In sell, print first, outside any lock.
Then guard only the adding with a synchronized block on this.
hints: The lesson shows a lock on a whole method and a lock on a few lines of it. Here only one line needs the lock.

A block names the object whose lock it takes: the Takings itself, as a synchronized method does. A BigDecimal never changes, so reading the takings, adding and keeping the new value all belong inside the block.
`printer.print(fare);` then `synchronized (this) { total = total.add(fare); }`, and `synchronized BigDecimal total() { return total; }`.
